name: Nyanza
lede: Nyanza is a very pale yellow-green, named, by most accounts, for the Swahili word for "lake" that once labeled East Africa's Great Lakes on colonial-era maps.

sections.title: A lake-country word
sections.body:
*Nyanza* is Bantu and Swahili for "lake," and the word was long attached to the African Great Lakes; Lake Victoria appeared on nineteenth-century maps as "Victoria Nyanza" [1]. Our sources do not record who first attached the word to this particular pale green, so the link to lake-country scenery is a reasonable reading, not a documented fact [1].

The swatch itself is older on paper than that story: Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary of color names lists it at plate 19, cell C4, and its editors traced the name's first recorded use back to 1892 [2]. The nearest look-alikes on file are [[pale-blue-green]] and [[tea-green]], both darker, and [[honeydew]] and [[oural-green|Oural Green]], duller and greener [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A close match to this green turns up in 7 of our 23,781 archived paintings, about 0.03 per cent, with the within-painting lens finding it in 3; that is rarer than 81 per cent of our named colors [4]. In printed English the word *nyanza* itself peaks in the 1890s and climbs fastest from the 1860s, a Google Books curve that covers every sense of the word, including the lake and the place name, not only the color; the archive counts above are as photographed, a screen-color match, not a pigment test [4].

origin.named_after: Swahili nyanza, "lake," as in the old name Victoria Nyanza for Lake Victoria (reading, not a documented fact)
origin.source: Maerz & Paul, A Dictionary of Color (1930)
